title: Compound Interest
subtitle: Why money grows like a snowball. Two short quests, one formula decoded symbol by symbol, live sliders.
about: This is the demo course that ships with the gamify-learn skill. It is original content written to show every step type: predict, idea, decoder, worked example, lab, brain dump, quiz, flashcards.

glossary.meaning: The money you start with: the first deposit. Everything else is built on top of it.
A fee the bank pays you for keeping money with them, written as a percent of your balance per year.
Interest paid only on the original principal. Same dollar amount every year, so growth is a straight line.
Interest paid on the principal plus all interest already earned. Growth speeds up, so the graph is a curve.
The yearly interest rate written as a decimal: 10% is 0.10, 5% is 0.05.
How many times per year the interest is added to the balance: 1 = yearly, 4 = quarterly, 12 = monthly, 365 = daily.
How long the money stays invested, in years.
The balance at the end: principal plus all interest.
The small raised number in x^k. It says multiply x by itself k times. 1.1^3 = 1.1 x 1.1 x 1.1.
The true yearly growth after compounding. 10% compounded daily is really about 10.52% a year.
How many years until money doubles at a given rate.
Quick mental estimate: years to double is about 72 divided by the rate as a whole percent.
The rate at which prices rise, so the same money buys less each year.
Your interest rate minus inflation: how fast your buying power actually grows.

quests.title: Money that makes money
outcomes: Explain the difference between simple and compound interest in one sentence
Say what every symbol in A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) means and what happens when it changes
Compute a balance by hand and check it against the sliders

steps.prompt: You put $1,000 in an account paying 10% a year and leave it for 30 years. Do you end up with about $4,000, $9,000 or $17,000?
steps.answer: About **$17,400**. Most people guess $4,000 because they think in straight lines. Interest that earns interest is not a straight line, and that gap is this whole quest.

steps.title: Simple interest: the boring baseline
lines: You deposit money. That first deposit is the **principal**.
Every year the bank pays a percent of the **original** deposit only.
steps.analogy: A tap dripping at a constant speed into a bucket. Twice as long, twice as much water.
steps.example: $1,000 at 10% simple: year 1 = $1,100, year 2 = $1,200 ... year 30 = $4,000. A straight line.
steps.keep: Simple interest = same dollars every year.

steps.title: Compound interest: interest earns interest
lines: Each year's interest is **added to the balance**.
Next year the percent is taken from the **bigger** balance.
So the growth itself grows. The graph is a curve, not a line.
steps.analogy: A snowball rolling downhill. The bigger it gets, the more snow it picks up on every turn.
steps.trap: Compounding is not a higher rate. It is the **same rate** applied to a **growing balance**.

steps.title: Decode the compound interest formula
steps.intro: One line of symbols. Here is what each piece IS, in plain words, and what it does to the answer.
steps.read: A equals P times one-plus-r-over-n, raised to the power n times t.

parts.name: AMOUNT (the answer)
parts.plain: How much money you have at the end: your starting money plus all the interest.
parts.effect: It is what you solve for. Bigger P, r, n or t all push A up.

parts.name: PRINCIPAL (what you start with)
parts.effect: Double P and A exactly doubles. P scales everything but never changes how fast it grows.

parts.name: RATE (yearly interest)
parts.plain: The yearly interest rate as a decimal. 10% is 0.10.
parts.effect: Higher r bends the curve upward. 6% vs 8% looks tiny but explodes over decades.

parts.name: COMPOUNDS PER YEAR
parts.plain: How many times a year interest is added: 1 = yearly, 12 = monthly, 365 = daily.
parts.effect: More often helps, but only a little: 10% compounded daily is about 10.52% a year, not 20%.

parts.name: TIME (in years)
parts.plain: How long the money stays invested.
parts.effect: t sits in the exponent, so every extra year multiplies the balance again. Time is the strongest lever.

steps.note: **r/n** cuts the yearly rate into n smaller slices. **n x t** counts how many slices happen in total. Each slice multiplies your balance by (1 + r/n).
steps.trap: Type r as **0.10**, not 10. If you use 10 you are claiming 1000% interest.

steps.title: Worked example: compute it by hand
steps.problem: You deposit **$2,000** at **6%** a year, compounded **monthly**, for **5 years**. What is A?
steps.answer: A is about **$2,697.70**. Interest earned: about $697.70.

steps.title: Lab: pull every lever yourself
steps.intro: Red = compound, blue = simple. Move one slider at a time and watch which output changes.
tries: Set t = 5, then 20, then 40. Where does the red curve pull away from the blue line?
Drop r to 3%, then raise it to 12%. Which slider bends the curve most?
Move n from 1 to 12. How big is the change in A, really?
Double P. Does A exactly double?
steps.keep: Time and rate bend the curve. Principal only scales it. n barely matters.

steps.prompt: Without looking: explain compound interest and what A, P, r, n and t mean.
points: Interest is paid on principal + earlier interest (snowball)
A = final amount, P = starting deposit
r = yearly rate as a decimal (0.10 for 10%)
n = compounds per year, t = years
t is in the exponent, so time is the strongest lever
More frequent compounding (n) helps only slightly

quiz.answer: Interest is calculated on the starting deposit plus all interest already earned
wrong: Interest is calculated only on the starting deposit
The bank raises the rate every year
Interest is paid once, at the end
quiz.why: Compound means the interest is added to the balance, so the next interest payment is bigger. Paying only on the starting deposit is simple interest.

quiz.q: In A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), what does n stand for?
quiz.answer: How many times per year interest is added to the balance
wrong: The number of deposits you make
The interest rate as a percent
quiz.why: n counts compounding periods per year (12 = monthly). The number of years is t, and the rate is r.

quiz.q: You write r = 5 for a 5% rate in the formula. What goes wrong?
quiz.answer: You are using 500% interest; it must be r = 0.05
wrong: Nothing, the formula accepts whole percents
quiz.why: The formula wants a decimal. 5% = 5/100 = 0.05. Plugging in 5 means 500%.

quiz.q: $1,000 at 10% simple interest for 3 years. What is the balance?
quiz.why: Simple interest adds $100 per year for 3 years: $1,300. $1,331 is the compound answer (1,000 x 1.1^3).

quiz.q: You double P and change nothing else. What happens to A?
wrong: A more than doubles because of compounding
A grows by the interest rate
quiz.why: P is a plain multiplier in front of the formula, so doubling P doubles A. Compounding changes the growth rate, not the scaling.

quiz.q: 10% compounded daily instead of yearly changes the yearly growth to about:
quiz.why: (1 + 0.10/365)^365 is about 1.1052, so about 10.52%. It helps a little. It does not double the rate.

quiz.q: Why is time (t) the strongest lever in the formula?
quiz.answer: t is in the exponent, so every extra year multiplies the balance again
wrong: t is the largest number in the formula
Longer time raises the interest rate
quiz.why: Exponents repeat multiplication. Each extra year multiplies the whole balance by the same growth factor, so the effect stacks.

cards.back: Simple: % of the original deposit only (line). Compound: % of deposit + earned interest (curve).

cards.front: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt): what is A?

cards.back: Principal: the starting deposit. It only scales the answer.

cards.front: How do you type r for 7%?

cards.back: n = compounds per year (12 = monthly). t = years.

cards.front: Which symbol is the strongest lever and why?
cards.back: t: it is in the exponent, so every extra year multiplies the balance again.

lines: Compound interest = interest on interest: a curve, not a line.
A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt): P scales, r and t bend, n helps a little.
Always use r as a decimal.
recap.teach: Explain to a friend why $1,000 at 10% becomes ~$17,400 in 30 years and not $4,000.

quests.title: Rule of 72, inflation and starting early
outcomes: Estimate doubling time in your head with the Rule of 72
Explain why inflation is compounding working against you
Show with numbers why starting early beats starting big

steps.prompt: Roughly how many years does it take money to double at 8% a year? 5, 9 or 15?
steps.answer: About **9 years**. There is a shortcut that gets you there in your head. That is the next screen.

steps.title: Decode the Rule of 72
steps.read: Years to double is about 72 divided by the rate.

parts.name: DOUBLING TIME
parts.plain: How many years until your money is twice what it was.
parts.effect: Higher rate means fewer years to double.

parts.name: THE MAGIC NUMBER
parts.plain: About 69.3 (that is 100 x ln 2) rounded up to 72 because 72 divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12.
parts.effect: It is fixed. It never changes.

parts.name: RATE AS A WHOLE PERCENT
parts.effect: Double the rate and you halve the years.

steps.trap: Here r is a **whole number** (8). In the compound formula r was a **decimal** (0.08). Different tools, different units.

steps.title: Worked example: double and quadruple
steps.problem: Money grows at **6%** a year. How long to double? How long to become 4 times as big?

steps.label: 4x = two doublings
steps.work: double once, then double again: 12 + 12 = 24 years

steps.answer: Doubles in about **12 years**, quadruples in about **24 years**.

steps.title: Lab: how good is the Rule of 72?
steps.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 640 110' width='100%'><text x='6' y='24' font-size='17' font-family='monospace' fill='#12213f'>Rule of 72</text><rect x='130' y='6' width='{{min(72/r*20,500)}}' height='24' fill='#e63946' stroke='#12213f' stroke-width='3'/><text x='6' y='64' font-size='17' font-family='monospace' fill='#12213f'>Exact</text><rect x='130' y='46' width='{{min(log(2)/log(1+r/100)*20,500)}}' height='24' fill='#1f7fd1' stroke='#12213f' stroke-width='3'/><text x='130' y='98' font-size='14' font-family='monospace' fill='#40527a'>bar length = years to double (20 px per year, capped)</text></svg>
tries: Try 2%, 8% and 18%. Where are the estimate and the exact answer closest?
Find the year where the curve crosses 2. Does it match the number above?
steps.keep: Rule of 72 is a quick estimate. It is closest at middling rates.

steps.title: Inflation: the same math, working against you
lines: Prices compound too. At 3% inflation prices double in about **24 years** (72 / 3).
Money sitting in a drawer buys less every year.
What counts is your **real return**: your interest rate minus inflation.
steps.analogy: A leaking bucket. Each day's leak looks tiny, but the level keeps dropping.
steps.keep: Real return is about interest rate minus inflation rate.
steps.trap: Savings paying 3% when inflation is 4% means your buying power is **shrinking** by about 1% a year.

steps.title: Start early beats start big
lines: Ana puts **$5,000** in at age 25. Ben puts **$5,000** in at age 35.
Both earn 7% a year until age 65 and add nothing else.
Ana's money compounds for 40 years, Ben's for 30.
steps.example: Ana: 5,000 x 1.07^40 = **about $74,900**. Ben: 5,000 x 1.07^30 = **about $38,100**. Same deposit, almost double the result, because of 10 extra years.
steps.keep: Time is in the exponent. Money is only the multiplier.

steps.prompt: Without looking: Rule of 72, inflation, and why starting early wins.
points: Years to double is about 72 / rate (whole percent)
Double the rate halves the doubling time
Inflation is compounding against you; real return is rate minus inflation
Starting early wins because t is in the exponent

quiz.q: Rule of 72: about how many years to double money at 9%?
quiz.why: 72 / 9 = 8. The most common slip is to answer 9 because the rate is 9.

quiz.q: In years = 72 / r, how do you enter an 8% rate?
quiz.why: The Rule of 72 uses whole percents. The compound-interest formula uses decimals. Mixing them up is the classic mistake.

quiz.q: Money doubles in 12 years. How long until it is 4 times the original?
quiz.why: 4x is two doublings: 2 x 2. Two doublings take 12 + 12 = 24 years.

quiz.q: Inflation is 4% and your savings pay 3%. Your buying power:
quiz.why: Real return is roughly rate minus inflation: 3% - 4% = -1%. You have more dollars but they buy less.

quiz.q: Ana invests $5,000 at 25 and Ben $5,000 at 35, both at 7% to age 65. Ana ends with about:
quiz.why: 1.07^40 = 14.97 and 1.07^30 = 7.61, a ratio of about 1.97. Ten extra years in the exponent nearly doubles the result.

quiz.q: Why is the Rule of 72 using 72 and not 69?
quiz.answer: 72 is close to 69.3 and divides evenly by many common rates
wrong: 72 is the number of months in 6 years
72 is the average stock market return
quiz.why: The exact number is about 69.3 (100 x ln 2). 72 is easier because it divides by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12, and it is more accurate near 8%.

cards.back: Years to double is about 72 / rate (as a whole percent).

cards.front: Double the rate: what happens to doubling time?
How do you enter 8% in the Rule of 72 vs in the compound formula?

cards.back: Interest rate minus inflation rate: how fast buying power grows.

cards.front: Why does starting early beat starting big?
cards.back: Time is in the exponent, so each extra year multiplies the balance again.

lines: 72 / rate (whole percent) is about the years to double.
Inflation is compounding against you; look at real return.
Time in the exponent beats extra dollars.
recap.teach: Tell a friend how long their money takes to double at 6% and why waiting 10 years to start costs so much.
